captions: Part two. The strategies.
These charts use illustrative synthetic data.
They are not backtests, history, or recommendations.
Synthetic examples let us see the rule clearly.
They do not show a return.

Real markets add noise, queues, spreads, gaps, and
competition.
Momentum asks whether a move is persistent.
One common rule compares a fast moving average with
a slow moving average.
When the fast line rises above the slow line,
the rule can permit a long position.
When it falls back below, the rule exits or
reverses.
The chart is illustrative synthetic data.
Its failure mode is chop.

In a sideways market, repeated crosses create
whipsaws.

The system pays spread, slippage, and charges while
repeatedly
being wrong.
The important discipline is consistency.

A trend follower cannot celebrate one winner and
skip
the next valid signal.
That would replace a rule with hindsight.
The rule needs a position size and a loss
limit too.
Mean reversion starts from a different belief.
A price far from its recent average may move
back toward it.

Bollinger bands frame a moving average with
volatility bands.
R S I is an oscillator from zero to
one hundred.
A low reading or lower-band poke can become an
entry condition.
The chart is illustrative synthetic data.
But a strong trend can keep going.
Cheap can become cheaper.
A band is a measurement, not a floor.
Mean reversion needs a definition of normal.
That definition is always historical and imperfect.
Before trading it, ask what news or regime could
make the old average irrelevant.
